title: The Twilight of the Francis Fukuyama Era
gist: Suri reviews Fukuyama's memoir 'In the Realm of the Last Man', arguing Fukuyama's 'boredom/recognition' explanation for authoritarianism is wrong: populist authoritarianism rose because voters believed liberal democracy and open markets failed them, and it now constitutes a coherent alternative ideology.

insights.claim: Fukuyama argues democratic backsliding is driven by activists who reject being 'Last Men' in prosperous but meaningless liberal societies, citing Jan. 6 rioters as middle-class people seeking struggle for its own sake.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: One framework for persistent populist demand despite economic prosperity.
insights.quote: “Democratic backsliding,” he writes, “is driven by activists who do not want to be ‘Last Men’ tinkering with the house that has been built for them at the end of history.”

insights.claim: Liberal democracies depend on expert-run bureaucracies such as the Federal Reserve and university admissions offices, whose impersonal decisions breed resentment and a cleavage between the empowered and the humiliated.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Explains political pressure on technocratic institutions like central banks.
insights.locator: But bureaucracy is boring and impersonal

insights.claim: Fukuyama warns against 'repatrimonialization', whereby tribes, families, and affinity groups hoard resources and destroy competent, inclusive state institutions, which he sees as contemporary authoritarians' goal.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Erosion of institutional quality raises governance and policy risk.

insights.claim: Fukuyama's memoir offers little practical advice beyond calls to replace 'procedural fetishism' with respect-building leadership and civic institutions, which Suri dismisses as handwringing.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Liberal establishment lacks a compelling counter-program.

insights.claim: Suri argues authoritarians rose not because people were bored or disrespected but because large numbers of citizens believed liberal democracy did not work after losing homes, jobs, and health to open-market decisions.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Populism is rooted in economic grievance, implying durable protectionist policy demand.

insights.claim: The crises of the early 21st century, including global terrorism, failed Middle East wars, and the financial crash, were facilitated by post-1989 opening that sped flows of money, weapons, and radical ideas.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Openness carries systemic tail risks that fuel political backlash.

insights.claim: The authoritarian model of the last decade, national chauvinism, protectionism, and pervasive surveillance as in Xi's China, is a coherent and effective alternative to liberal democracy, not merely anti-liberal.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Ideological competition is structural, not a passing phase; affects trade and governance regimes.
insights.quote: The authoritarian model of the last decade is not just anti-liberal, it is a coherent and effective alternative

insights.claim: Trump's tariffs and trade wars, even with Canada, reflect authoritarians' rejection of free trade, a cornerstone of liberalism.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Protectionism is ideological, so likely persistent.

insights.claim: Post-1989 Russia and China adapted toward Western ideals for self-preservation rather than ideological capitulation, so communism's collapse never guaranteed liberal democracy's permanent triumph.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Expect convergence assumptions about rival powers to keep failing.

insights.claim: The legitimacy of some authoritarians has also declined as they start unwinnable wars and damage their economies, leaving people everywhere searching for new ideas, parties, and leaders.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Signals ongoing political volatility and churn in both democracies and autocracies.

insights.claim: The 'age of Fukuyama', marked by overconfident pursuit of liberal-capitalist hegemony, ran roughly from 1989 to 2024 and has now ended, opening a new beginning of history.
insights.speaker: Jeremi Suri
insights.so_what: Regime shift: assumptions of the globalization era no longer hold.
insights.quote: Perhaps Hegel would counsel that instead of the end of history and the last man, we should prepare for a new beginning of history
